claims.text: The initial material is zirconium-alloy cladding coated with elemental Cr.
Elemental Cr coatings on zirconium-alloy cladding can fail during elevated-temperature steam exposure.
Premature failure of the baseline coating is caused by elevated-temperature Cr-Zr interdiffusion.
The baseline Cr coating is protective under normal PWR water and high-temperature steam when those regimes are considered individually.
An interlayer of TiN on the order of tens of nanometers should be deposited between the zirconium alloy and elemental Cr coating.
A nanoscale TiN interlayer acts as a diffusion barrier at the Cr-Zr interface.
The TiN interlayer limits atomic transport of Cr and Zr across the coating-substrate interface.
TiN has sufficiently high thermal stability for the proposed nuclear-cladding exposures.
TiN has sufficiently low diffusivity to impede Cr-Zr interdiffusion at high temperature.
Suppressing Cr-Zr interdiffusion maintains the integrity of the Cr layer.
The TiN barrier prevents formation of deleterious intermetallic phases at the interface.
Interfacial intermetallic phases would weaken the coating under normal and accident conditions.
Relative to the unmodified Cr-coated baseline, the TiN interlayer will significantly reduce Cr-Zr interdiffusion.
Relative to the unmodified baseline, the TiN interlayer will enhance coating adhesion.
The TiN-modified coating will maintain oxidation resistance under both long-term PWR water and short-term high-temperature steam exposure.
The TiN interlayer will improve the durability of elemental Cr coatings across both normal PWR and accident-relevant steam regimes.
Subcritical water at approximately 315 degrees Celsius is representative of standard PWR operating conditions.
Steam exposure at approximately 1200 degrees Celsius is representative of an accident-relevant ATF transient.
The magnitude of the proposed improvement depends on TiN thickness and processing parameters.
